Joseph was taking the party to London to catch the high-speed railway service Eurostar and begin a "dream holiday" in Europe when the crash happened.
All the vehicles were travelling in the same direction on the south-bound carriageway of the M1 in what turned out to be the worse crash Britain has witnessed since 1993, when 12 schoolchildren and their teacher died in a minibus accident on the M40 motorway.
The assumption must be that the minibus, which was "flattened", was hit from behind and squeezed underneath the trailer of the heavy goods vehicle in front. Both the lorry drivers have been charged, one of them for being drunk.
Ryszard Masierak, 31, of Evesham, Worcestershire, is accused of eight counts of causing death by dangerous driving, four counts of causing serious injury by dangerous driving and eight counts of causing death by careless driving while over the prescribed alcohol limit. He has been remanded in custody to appear at High Wycombe Magistrates' Court on Monday.
David Wagstaff, 53, of Derwent Street, Stoke-on-Trent, is charged with eight counts of causing death by dangerous driving and four counts of causing serious injury by dangerous driving. He was bailed to appear at Milton Keynes Magistrates' Court on September 11.
Pictures of the vehicles appeared to show a FedEx lorry with its cab crushed and the cab of an AIM Logistics lorry twisted around to the side. Another image showed what appeared to be the crumpled wreckage of the minibus on the back of a flatbed truck. Broken glass and debris from the collision was scattered across the tarmac.
Chief inspector Henry Parsons, from the joint operations unit for roads policing, said: "Eight people lost their lives, with four seriously injured.... Officers are working to inform the next of kin of the people who died and specially trained family liaison officers will be offering them their support. Some of those involved were visiting the UK from India and we are working to keep families abroad informed."
A spokesman for the South Central Ambulance Service confirmed paramedics were called to the crash site at 3.12am on Saturday. "Sadly there have been several fatalities. We have treated four patients for serious or life-threatening injuries who have been taken to hospitals in Milton Keynes, Coventry and Birmingham," he said.
Wipro said three of its employees were among those who died, and a fourth staff member had been critically injured. "It is with deep regret and sadness that we confirm the passing away of three of our colleagues, Karthikeyan Ramasubramaniyam Pugalur, Rishi Rajeev Kumar, and Vivek Bhaskaran in a tragic road accident in the UK," a spokesman for the company said. "Our thoughts and prayers are with the families of all those who lost their lives in this tragedy."
It is understood the men were all contracted to work in Nottingham.

A forensic examination of the eight engineering students from Tamil Nadu who died in the accident on National Highway 66 at Kaipamangalam Panambikunnu, Thrissur, has found that most of the victims had consumed alcohol.

The expert also called for a comprehensive investigation into other possible contributing factors.
Concerns have been raised over safety lapses at the NH66 construction site and the alleged unsafe parking of heavy vehicles along the roadside, which could have increased the severity of the accident.

Following a complaint from locals to the Vadanappilly police, the students allegedly left the area.
Police are collecting CCTV footage, including footage from around the Tenth Stone area, to establish the sequence of events before the crash.
Dr Hithesh Shanker said the tragedy should not be attributed to a single factor without scientific investigation, stressing that all possible contributing circumstances need to be examined.

Tamil Nadu has reported a significant reduction in fatal road accidents with the number of deaths coming down by 273 in 2024 compared to the previous year. Corrective measures in Black Spots or accident-prone zones, effective enforcement of traffic rules and intensive drive against drunken driving contributed to the declining trend in fatal road accidents.
Despite the increase in human and vehicle population and length of roads across the State, the State police undertook a series of impactful initiatives to prevent road accidents and bring about safety, Director-General of Police & Head of the Police Force, Shankar Jiwal, said on Friday.
Rectifying design defects or other corrective measures along National/State Highways, issuing ‘challans’ to violators of traffic rules and stringent action against rash and negligent driving and intensified patrolling of accident-prone zones helped in bringing down the number of road accidents. While 18,347 people died in 17,526 fatal road accidents in 2023, the number came down to 18,074 and 17,282 respectively last year.
Driver’s error
An analysis of fatal accident cases in 2023 revealed that in 16,800 of the total 17,526 incidents, driver’s error was the cause. As part of the steps to address the issue, ‘Highway Patrol Mobile Application’ was used extensively by the traffic police for providing road safety awareness and enforcement of road safety rules. The police identified 6,165 Black Spots after conducting a field survey where ground conditions were assessed on the basis of vehicle density, traffic environment and number of accidents.
Road safety engineering measures were implemented in association with the State Highways Department to enhance safety. Of the 6,165 Black Spots, short term action was taken in 3,165 locations to reduce the speed of vehicles. A majority of the cities and districts had shown reduction in road accidents, he said.
U-turn system
Mr. Jiwal said that U-turn system implemented in Coimbatore City in consultation with the Highways Department had led to a reduction of fatalities in road accidents by 4%. As part of the programme, U-turns were introduced replacing signals at junctions resulting in better vehicular movement. A similar approach was being tried in other cities, including Chennai.
Last year, a total of 12.58 lakh cases were booked of which 2.07 lakh cases were registered against those overspeeding driving, 2.58 lakh cases against road users jumping the red signal and 4.20 lakh cases involving people found to be using their mobile phones while driving. 12,306 people were booked on charges of drunken driving. The State traffic police registered 64.94 lakh cases against people not wearing helmets and 5.78 lakh cases involving those not wearing seat belts.
Suspension of driving licences
After the State police wrote to the transport authorities recommending the suspension of driving licences belonging to 3.49 lakh individuals for violating the motor vehicle rules, 80,558 driving licences were suspended.
Mr. Jiwal said highway patrol vehicles had rescued 12,629 people who were critically injured in road accidents and rushed them to the nearest hospital within the Golden Hour.
Besides stringent enforcement of traffic rules which would also serve as a deterrence to irresponsible use of road infrastructure and negligent driving endangering fellow road users, thousands of awareness programmes were conducted to educate road users on safe and responsible driving.

Losing His Brother Inspired Him to Offer Free Ambulances & Feed 1.5 Lakh People in Tamil Nadu

In 2008, Durai Prithviraj’s younger brother met with a fatal accident near Aruppukottai, 20 km from their home in Tamil Nadu’s Virudhunagar district.
“There was no ambulance or hearse van nearby. I had to pay a large sum just to get his body home and conduct his last rites,” recalls Durai.
Haunted by this, Durai kept thinking: What would poor families do in such a situation? That thought stayed with him for years.
After graduating in 2011, Durai became a village administrative officer. From his modest salary, he began saving every month to buy a van.
“I’d save almost 50 percent of my earnings. I also spent from my own pocket to help people with food, clothes, medicines and more,” he says.
In 2018, he bought a second-hand Omni for Rs 1.8 lakh. He raised more funds to modify it with a bed and first-aid kits to run as an ambulance.
“We offer free rides to those who can’t afford it. Those who can, give what they wish. It helps with fuel and maintenance,” says Durai.
His NGO, Rajesh Udhavum Karangal, now runs three free ambulances helping people within 40 km — sometimes even up to 100 km away.
Inspired by his work, donors began supporting him. One even gifted a second-hand van, now named ‘Aandalammavin Thunai’ in memory of his grandmother.
Durai also converted part of his home into a shelter. Volunteers help cook and serve three meals a day to hundreds of people.
So far, they have provided over 1.5 lakh free meals to the underprivileged through Rajesh Udhavum Karangal.

Following the deaths of three children when their school bus was hit by a passenger train at a manned level crossing in Cuddalore district of Tamil Nadu on July 8, Union Railway Minister Ashwini Vaishnaw announced that all manned non-interlocking level crossings in India will be converted to interlocking level crossings. This will be a challenging task, given the vast numbers of such gates in the broad gauge section and the Railways’ safety track record.
An interlocking network locks the gates to the signals and is a crucial safety system. Non-interlocking gates are not connected to the signalling system, requiring a person to open and shut the gates to allow a train to pass through safely. There are 17,083 manned level crossings on the broad gauge network, according to 2024 Railway data. Even on national highways, 417 manned level crossings are yet to be eliminated, according to a Railways Standing Committee report of 2024-25.
Also Read | Three major rail accidents in three years: What is the government doing?
Vaishnaw made the announcement when he reviewed “critical Railway safety issues” on July 9, the day after the Tamil Nadu incident, when a decision was taken to implement 11 key actions regarding level crossings. The Minister also wanted CCTV and recording systems installed at all level crossings.
Implementation challenges
While the announcement is welcome, implementation might prove far more difficult. Only in 2019 was the task of converting all unmanned level crossings on broad gauge to manned crossings—a critical safety issue in India—completed. According to data the Railways Ministry presented in Parliament, between 2014 and 2019, 8,948 unmanned level crossings on the broad gauge network were eliminated by manning, closure/merger, or construction of road overbridges/underbridges. Despite its top priority, the task took five years to complete.
According to Indian Railway data, of the over 17,000 manned level crossings in the broad gauge network, the largest number, as of April 1, 2024, is in Uttar Pradesh, at 2,889. Bihar takes second place (1,786), West Bengal (1,635) and Gujarat (1,432) come third and fourth, while Tamil Nadu with 1,285 is fifth. The budget allocation under the head “Road safety level crossings and Road Over Bridge/Road Under Bridge” for 2024-25 (Budget Estimate) is Rs.9,980 crore.
In August 2019, The Hindu reported that Southern Railway planned to interlock all manned level crossings. “In 2020-21, Southern Railway will take up interlocking of manned gates in the Tiruchi and Madurai divisions... To start with, engineers plan to completely convert manned level crossing gates in the Chennai, Salem and Palghat divisions by the end of this financial year [2021-22].”
The July 8 accident occurred in Cuddalore, which is in Tiruchi division. Clearly, the task set for 2020-21 was not undertaken.
In December 2024, in response to an unstarred question in the Lok Sabha, Vaishnaw said: “As of 01.04.2024, there are 17,083 manned level crossings on the broad gauge network of Indian Railways... Sanctioning works of road overbridge/road underbridge in lieu of level crossings is a continuous and dynamic process of Indian Railways. Such works are prioritised and taken up on the basis of impact on safety in train operations, mobility of trains, impact for road users, and feasibility.”
The Minister further stated that between 2021 and 2024, the number of road overbridges and underbridges constructed was 3,139. As of April 1, 2024, 4,200 overbridges and underbridges were sanctioned, at a cost of Rs.92,692 crore.
The Minister also detailed the steps taken by Indian Railways to minimise rail accidents at level crossings. He said level crossings with high rail or road traffic were being interlocked with signals to enhance safety; that inspection drives were being launched periodically to ensure availability of basic infrastructure at level crossings such as whistle boards, road warning boards, and speed breakers; and that awareness campaigns and safety slogans were being used to spread safety consciousness among road users.

The Cuddalore accident is not isolated. On June 22, a goods train hit an autorickshaw at a manned level crossing gate in Rajasthan. A 2023-24 report of the Standing Committee on Railways presented in Parliament in December 2024 noted that it was the stated aim of the Railways to eliminate manned level crossings to enhance safety and mobility. “The feasibility of these projects relies on various factors, including State government consent for level crossing closures, availability of land for approach roads, and public support,” it said.
In a statement released on July 8, Southern Railway said that it had sanctioned a fully-funded underpass on the gate where the accident occurred, but that for the past one year it had not received the Cuddalore District Collector’s permission to proceed.
The blame game between Tamil Nadu and the Union government has begun over who shares major responsibility for the tragedy.

‘I called out to dad, but he wasn’t responding’: Shine Tom Chacko on fatal crash, says he got 30 stitches, cracked his back
For the first time, Shine Tom Chacko has opened up about the tragic accident that injured him and took life of his father, CP Chacko.
Actor Shine Tom Chacko was involved in a serious car accident in Dharmapuri near Salem, Tamil Nadu, in June. The actor lost his father, C.P. Chacko (73), in the accident. Photos and videos of a heartbroken Shine bidding farewell to his father had surfaced on the internet. Now, for the first time, the actor has opened up about the fatal incident and how he is coping with his father’s death.
‘I opened my eyes, the vehicle had already crashed’
In an interview with The Cue, Shine Tom Chacko said, “So I was lying in the back seat. I’d wake up from sleep and ask daddy for a biscuit. daddy gave me a biscuit two or three times. Then, when I opened my eyes, the vehicle had already crashed. I was in the back. After that, daddy never communicated with any of us again.”
Shine shared that the accident happened so suddenly that they didn’t even realise they were lying on the road. “Mommy is asking, ‘Why are we lying on this road? Where are we going?’ Until then, an accident was just a sight to me. But when you go through it yourself…I truly broke down and cried, standing on the road, ‘Someone please come and help, someone please get us to the hospital,'” he said.
Shin Tom Chacko revealed that although his brother — Joe John Chacko — was sitting in the front seat, he was left unharmed. He said, “My brother, Joe was sitting in the front. Joe didn’t even have a scratch. I was thinking, ‘How is he walking around like this, unharmed? Will he walk and then collapse or something?’ Because the car was completely wrecked. I called out to daddy, but he wasn’t responding.”
‘There are 10 to 30 stitches’
Shine Tom Chacko also mentioned that he isn’t sure about some of the details, as he had taken medication to help him sleep, as part of his rehab. He said that because he was on these medications, his father would never allow him to drive the vehicle. Shine also revealed that he received 30 stitches after being badly injured in the accident. He said, “I asked the doctor, ‘Will there be about 10 stitches?’ The doctor said, ’10? There are 10 to 30 stitches.'” Shine also shared that he had a small crack in his back due to the accident. On the other hand, his brother Joe had seatbelt injuries. Explaining the same, he said, “Even if you wear a seatbelt, from the impact of the crash, you get chest pains. Those will gradually go away.”
Speaking about his mother suffering from a hip injury, he said, “Mommy’s dislocated hip was relocated and put back in place. Now she’s lying down. There’s a small crack in her hip.”
Shine Tom Chacko shared that his mother hasn’t fully accepted his father’s death and often asks his whereabouts. However, the actor’s brothers and sisters have been there for them.
About the accident
Shine Tom Chacko was travelling with his family — his father CP Chacko, mother Mariya and brother Joe — along with their driver Aneesh, to Bengaluru when their car was hit by a lorry coming from the opposite direction. CP Chacko died on the spot, while Shine, Mariya, Jo, and the driver were rushed to a nearby hospital. While Mariya sustained a serious hip injury in the accident, Shine suffered fractures below his left shoulder and on his spine.
After receiving medical attention, Shine and Mariya came directly from the hospital to their home in Mundar to perform the final rites of his father on June 9. Photos showed a teary-eyed Shine giving a final kiss to his father. The entire family, including Shine’s brother and sisters — Sumi and Riya — flew in from New Zealand to attend their father’s last rites.

Kundara: A 24-year-old engineer from Kerala, who suffered critical injuries in a motorcycle accident at Sriperumbudur in Tamil Nadu, has passed away. His decision to donate organs after being declared brain dead has helped save or improve the lives of 10 people.

After doctors at Apollo Hospital, Chennai, confirmed brain death, Arun’s parents consented to donate his organs. Through the donation, 10 people received a new lease of life. His two kidneys, two eyes, heart valves, liver, lungs, intestine, and skin were donated.
Arun had completed diploma in Mechanical Engineering from SN Polytechnic College, Kottiyam, and secured employment through campus placement. After leaving his first company, he joined HL Clemov India Private Limited, manufacturer of automobile spare parts in Sriperumbudur.

He was initially taken to a nearby private medical college hospital by co-workers. His family, who reached the hospital on Thursday evening, later shifted him to Apollo Hospital in Chennai.
Despite treatment, doctors declared him brain dead on Saturday. He was then transferred on ventilator support to Rajiv Gandhi Government General Hospital, Chennai, where preparations for organ donation began after obtaining the family's consent.
Following a surgery that lasted several hours, Arun’s organs were transplanted into 10 recipients. Details of the recipients will be shared with the family at a later stage.

General Bipin Rawat died along with his wife and 11 others, when their IAF Mi-17 crashed in Tamil Nadu on Wednesday.
The crash was second one in which a top general was killed after the 1993 accident in Sikkim that killed Eastern Command chief, Lt Gen Jameel Mahmood. Incidentally, both involved an Mi-17 helicopter, bad weather and the officer being accompanied by his wife.
Besides him, his wife, Military Assistant Col M.N. Ahmed, Lt Lakshman Tyagi, orderly Naik G. Thyagarajan, his personal bodyguard Havildar S. Vasudevan, and the IAF crew were also killed.
Commissioned into the Artillery in 1959, Mahmood commanded a platoon in Sikkim during the 1962 India-China war, and was conferred the Yudh Seva Medal. He also saw action during the 1965 and 1971 India-Pakistan war, held a series of key command (including of a brigade, infantry division, and the Srinagar-headquartered Chinar Corps), staff and instructional posts, including at the IMA, and the Army War College.
He became the Eastern Command chief in October 1992. Three decades back, the Indian Army and Air Force lost a host of senior officials when an IAF Alouette chopper crashed near Poonch in November 1963.
Western Command chief, Lt Gen Daulat Singh, Western Air Command chief, Air Vice Marshal Erlic Pinto, Chinar Corps Commander, Lt Gen Bikram Singh, 25 Infantry Division chief, Maj Gen N.K.D. Nanavati, and 93 Brigade chief, Brigadier S.R. Oberoi, as well as pilot, Flight Lt S.S. Sodhi, were killed in the crash.
However, the miraculous survival of all passengers of an IAF de Havilland Devon transport aircraft crash near Lucknow in February 1952 was a godsend to the Indian Army.
On board were future Army chiefs - Lt Gen S.M. Shrinagesh and Major Gen K.S. Thimayya -- as well as Major Gen S.P.P. Thorat, later Eastern Command chief, Maj Gen Sardanand Singh, Major Gen Mohinder Singh Chopra and Brig Ajaib Singh.
Lt Gen Shrinagesh's ADC had to give up his seat at the last moment to accommodate Brig Singh. The person was K. Sundarji, who would go on to head the Indian Army in his turn.

Abstract
This study presents a comprehensive analysis of road accidents in India by using official government data sets from 53 major cities across 28 states. This research is conducted under a Type-2 picture fuzzy environment with advanced aggregation operators such as the arithmetic mean, geometric mean, hamy mean, Einstein weighted operator, and Aczel-Alsina operator. To enhance decision-making under uncertainty, a novel distance measure is proposed and theoretically validated. Five prominent distance-based multi-criteria decision-making (MCDM) methods such as TOPSIS, VIKOR, WASPAS, CODAS, and COPRAS were applied to rank the cities based on 35 critical road accident-related criteria. The results of the model revealed that Chennai consistently secured the top ranking in TOPSIS, COPRAS, and FIR. Amritsar also performed exceptionally, ranking 1st in VIKOR and achieving 3rd in TOPSIS. In contrast, cities such as Kanpur, Lucknow, and Ahmedabad consistently ranked in the bottom quartile, with Kanpur receiving the lowest position (53rd) in TOPSIS and FIR, indicating they are in critical risk zones. Mid-ranked cities such as Hyderabad, Pune, and Rajkot showed variations across methods but maintained stable FIR positions. To validate the robustness of the rankings, a comprehensive sensitivity analysis was conducted by various decision parameter q, confirming the stability of rankings under fluctuating conditions. The proposed framework improved the precision of accident severity and demonstrated adaptability to broader decision-making scenarios involving uncertainty. This study contributes a novel, integrated, and mathematically rigorous methodology for assessing urban safety for policymakers to reduce the road accident risks across Indian cities.

Introduction
Road accidents are one of the leading causes of death and injury globally, posing a serious threat to public health and safety. According to the WHO report approximately 1.3 million people die each year as a result of road traffic crashes1. Millions more suffer non-fatal injuries, often leading to long-term disabilities and emotional trauma. The burden is disproportionately higher in low- and middle-income countries, where 93% of the world’s road fatalities occur despite having only 60% of the vehicles. Road accidents affect individuals, families and also the broader economy system. The economic cost of road traffic accidents is estimated at 3% of a country’s GDP in many nations. Emergency medical services, insurance payouts and productivity loss contribute significantly to these financial burdens. Children, young adults and working-age individuals are most vulnerable loss to the nation’s human capital. In urban areas traffic accidents contribute to congestion, delays and pollution. Globally road accidents are considered as a development issue and also a traffic concern2.
Preventing road accidents aligns with the UNSDG especially goal 3 (good health and well-being) and goal 11 (sustainable cities and communities). Enhanced infrastructure, proper urban planning and vehicle safety standards are key to reducing risks. Strong enforcement of traffic laws including penalties for drunk driving, speeding and mobile phone use has proven effective in many countries3. Public awareness and education campaigns play a crucial role in shaping road behavior. Vehicle maintenance and technological advancements such as ABS, lane-assist systems and collision warnings have improved safety4.
In many parts of the world roads have poor conditions, lack of enforcement and limited awareness. Data collection and research into road accident provides help in formulating effective policies. International cooperation and knowledge exchange strengthen global road safety efforts5. Developing nations are prioritising road safety in policy frameworks and budgets.
Road safety is a responsibility which involving governments, engineers, law enforcement and road users. Reducing accidents helps economic development with social well-being. Safer roads ensure better mobility, access to education and healthcare in both urban and rural areas. Addressing this issue can transform the path of people travel and live.
India has one of the highest rates of road accidents globally which providing continuous analysis and interventions. According to the MoRTH over 1.5 lakh people die in road crashes annually in India6. Road accidents in India have emerged as a critical public safety issue with severe socio-economic and health implications. These accidents lead to tragic loss of life and also result in millions of injuries. Most of these cause a long-term disability and trauma. These accidents cause loss of life and massive economic setbacks with long-term trauma for families. Most fatalities occur among the \(18-45\) age group which representing a significant loss of the productive workforce. India accounts for almost 11% of global road accident deaths despite having only 1% of the world’s vehicles.
Continuous data collection and analysis help to identify accident-prone zones, black spots across highways and urban roads. Poor road conditions, lack of signage and faulty design are common contributors to these high-risk areas. The government has initiated steps such as iRAD to monitor and reduce accidents. Speeding, drunk driving and non-compliance with helmet and seatbelt rules are among the leading human factors. Overloaded and poorly maintained vehicles contribute significantly to accident rates.
Urban traffic congestion in metros adds the chaos and increasing the risk of collisions. The rapid rise in vehicle ownership in two-wheelers needs for stronger safety regulations. The motor vehicles act 2019 introduced stricter penalties to improve driver discipline. Awareness campaigns such as sadak suraksha jeevan raksha aim to educate citizens on road safety. But enforcement is a challenge due to manpower shortages and inconsistent monitoring.
Advanced traffic systems with AI-based monitoring are implemented in smart cities. School and college-based road safety education programs are important to build long term awareness7. Regular vehicle fitness checks and driver training need to be standardised across states. Collaboration with NGOs and the private sector enhances outreach engagement. Salem8 proposed a multi-agent V2V communication framework to enhance vehicle dynamics and cooperative driving through intelligent information exchange among connected vehicles. Real-time data analysis using GPS, CCTV and mobile apps helps to generate quicker response and trend identification9. Thanasupsin et al.10 developed a nested logit model to analyse travel mode choice behaviour within university campuses by examining multiple transportation preferences and influencing factors. When system need decision support system it can utilise adaptive artificial intelligence learning models within decision support systems to improve intelligent regional management under dynamic and data-driven environments11. Fadwa12 developed an integrated framework for multi-level production defect detection by combining quality management tools with maintenance optimisation strategies to improve industrial performance. Also, Tiryaki and Oral13 developed an advanced traffic sign classification framework using spatial transformer networks integrated with convolutional neural networks to improve recognition accuracy in intelligent transportation systems.
Tamil Nadu and Gujarat shown a reduction in accident rates through focused action plans. Still rural areas face challenges due to poor infrastructure and delayed emergency services. Continuous analysis include social, geographical and behavioral factors unique to each region. Multi agency coordination among transport, police, health and urban development departments is vital. In India the analysis of road accidents involves uncertainty due to imprecise, incomplete data related to human behavior, road conditions and enforcement levels. To handle this uncertainty this model provides the framework of T2FS which allows for better modeling of the ambiguity present in expert opinions and accident-related factors. By incorporating aggregation operators diverse expert judgments and criteria can combine to evaluate accident prone areas. It introduces a novel distance measure designed for T2PF environments which enhances the precision of evaluations between alternatives. This integrated approach enables robust decision-making in identifying high risk zones and developing road safety interventions. Fuzzy sets
The concept of FS introduced by Zadeh in 196515. It was a groundbreaking step toward mathematical modeling and imprecision in real-world decision-making. Classical logic treats information in a binary manner but real-world problems such as economic forecasting and road accident analysis often involve vague data. FS addressed this by allowing partial membership and offering a flexible framework to capture gradations of truth which laid the foundation for several powerful extensions of fuzzy theory.
T1FS allow each element to have a degree of membership ranging from 0 to 1. But the membership of T2FS16 itself is uncertain such as when evaluating traffic risks and fluctuating economic indicators become essential. These sets model fuzziness in the membership function itself and providing an added layer of uncertainty modeling. IVT2FS17 are widely used due to their computational simplicity and effectiveness in capturing uncertainty ranges in problems.
To improve the representational accuracy of FS researchers have designed various fuzzy number shapes such as triangular, trapezoidal, pentagonal and heptagonal fuzzy numbers. Among these TrFNs are commonly employed for modeling economic intervals and estimating accident-related data that lie within approximate boundaries. Recently, Turgay et al.18 provided an uncertainty-aware evaluation framework based on T-spherical hesitant fuzzy rough sets for intelligent assessment of Edge-Cloud architectures in smart manufacturing.
Further enhancing the flexibility of fuzzy logic IFS19 introduce three components for each element. They are a degree of membership, non-membership and hesitation. This structure enables a deeper representation of expert uncertainty, such as in assessing regional economic instability or determining accident-prone zones where expert opinions may diverge. Several important extensions have emerged from this model:
- 
                    BIFS20 allow simultaneous representation of positive and negative perceptions which is valuable when analyzing conflicting public opinions about transportation safety.
- 
                    BVFS integrate both positive and negative contexts into a unified framework which useful in modeling dual-sided decision parameters.
- 
                    IVIFS accommodates ranges for both membership and non-membership values which ideal for capturing variability in economic metrics.
- 
                    T2IFS enhance capabilities by introducing non-membership to intuitionistic functions which suitable in high uncertainty domains.
Another milestone in fuzzy logic is the development of PyFS21. It extends IFN by allowing the sum of squares of membership and non-membership degrees to be at most 1. This extends the modeling capacity for highly uncertain environments. In applications such as urban traffic control, accident severity classification and economic impact assessment PyFS provides greater flexibility. It representing conflicting, incomplete and hesitant information. The evolution of FS theory from T1FS to advanced models such as T2FS, IFS and PyFS offers a powerful toolbox for analyzing complex socio-economic phenomena.
Literature review on MCDM methods in fuzzy environment
In recent decades MCDM methods have gained prominence for solving complex problems involving conflicting criteria. To better handle real-world uncertainty researchers have integrated MCDM methods with FS theory which leading to more flexible models. This review explores the evolution and application of various fuzzy-based MCDM approaches and highlighting their strengths, limitations and domains of use. Table 1 explains the recent works that used MCDM in the field of road accidents and economic strategy. Recently, Altayf et al.22 developed an MCDM framework for the intelligent selection of photovoltaic-battery energy storage systems (PV-BESS) by jointly evaluating cost and reliability factors. Mustafa et al.23 developed a GIS-based multi-criteria evaluation framework to assess land suitability for wind power farm development in Iraq by integrating environmental, spatial and technical factors. Chaoui et al.24 integrated geospatial technologies with multi-criteria decision analysis to enhance sustainable and resilient urban planning through comprehensive spatial and strategic evaluation. Qiu et al.25 developed a decision-making model for prioritising low-carbon policies by evaluating climate mitigation strategies under multiple sustainability criteria.
Motivation
Road traffic accidents in India have a severe public health concern and demanding immediate evaluation systems. Due to the inherent vagueness in expert assessments of accident-related factors traditional models having uncertainty. To address this issue this study proposes a novel decision-making framework based on T2PFS combined with advanced aggregation operators and a customized distance measure.
- 
                    This study motivated by the increasing level of road accidents in India. This critical issue demands investigation and an innovative assessment framework.
- 
                    Traditional statistical models are insufficient for handling the ambiguity, vagueness and subjectivity associated with real-world data. Hence it is important to explore an advanced fuzzy model to capture the imprecise nature of expert evaluations.
- 
                    Most existing models fail to consider the degree of hesitation in decision making. This motivation addresses the gap to utilise T2PFS which provides a richer structure for managing uncertainty, neutrality and disagreement in expert opinions.
- 
                    Road accident analysis involves multiple factors such as vehicle, infrastructure and environment. It makes traffic accident prioritisation as an ideal domain for applying MCDM methods. This motivated to structure the factors into a strong decision making framework.
- 
                    A motivation from the research opportunity is to develop novel aggregation operators and an innovative distance measure with the T2PFNs. It could enhance the precision of the final rankings.
-

- 
                    Beyond academic interest this work strongly driven by the potential social impact. This research can assist policymakers and transportation authorities in prioritising road safety interventions.
The proposed fuzzy MCDM approach provides a proper evaluation of road accident risk factors under uncertainty. By incorporating T2PF modeling with a tailored distance measure this study offers a valuable insights for policy design and accident prevention strategies. This research opens new directions for applying advanced fuzzy models in other complex and uncertainty domains of public decision making.

This study applies various fuzzy aggregation operators and a novel distance measure to assess 53 cities using 35 critical accident-related criteria.

Structure
This article is organised into five sections. “Preliminaries” introduces the preliminary concepts including the mathematical foundation of T2PFNs and the proposed aggregation operators such as arithmetic, geometric, Hamy mean, Einstein weighted and Aczel-Alsina. “Case study: multi-criteria evaluation of road accidentseverity across cities” presents the real world case study involving road accident data from 53 Indian cities with the detailed algorithm designed to evaluate the cities using MCDM methods. “Results and validation” offers a discussion covering the results obtained from TOPSIS, VIKOR, WASPAS, CODAS and COPRAS with a sensitivity analysis. This section highlights the strengths, comparative advantages and limitations of the proposed framework. “Sensitivity analysis” focuses on the validation of the results which proving the consistency of rankings, implications for urban safety planning and the effectiveness of the proposed method under varying decision parameters. Finally “Conclusion” concludes the study by summarising the key findings, confirming the robustness of the model and suggesting directions for future research in decision-making under uncertainty. Results and validation
The ranking of 53 Indian cities based on road accident data was performed using five well-established MCDM methods such as TOPSIS, VIKOR, WASPAS, CODAS and COPRAS. Each method produced an individual ranking list based on distinct criteria-weighted algorithms. Among all cities Chennai consistently showed lower severity values and received top positions across most methods. Specifically Chennai ranked 1st in TOPSIS, 3rd in VIKOR, 2nd in WASPAS, 2nd in CODAS and 1st in COPRAS. These consistent top ranks led Chennai to achieve the 1st place in the FIR64,65 and66 which confirming its outstanding road safety performance. Amritsar performed exceptionally well and securing ranks such as 3rd in TOPSIS and 1st in VIKOR and CODAS which reflects strong consistency in the results across diverse methods. Coimbatore and Chandigarh also maintained top 10 positions in most methods which demonstrating relatively safe traffic conditions and governance. Cities such as Kanpur, Lucknow and Ahmedabad consistently appeared in the bottom tier across all methods. For example Kanpur ranked 53rd in TOPSIS and 50th in VIKOR while Lucknow and Ahmedabad remained in the bottom 10 for all five methods. The rankings indicate road accident risks and the need of safety interventions.
Mid ranked cities such as Hyderabad, Pune and Rajkot showing the variations which reflecting their borderline performance and scope for improvement. To ensure the reliability of results the FIR calculated using an average rank aggregation across five methods. The FIR served as a comprehensive benchmark which is a minimising method in a specific bias and improving decision consistency. Cities with high ranks across methods maintained their position in the FIR which validating the robustness of the evaluation. The comparison revealed that top ranked cities in FIR such as Chennai, Amritsar and Coimbatore had lower sensitivity scores. It further validated the true values of their ranking. The cities with high FIR values corresponding to high sensitivity measures. This strong alignment between results and FIR ranking supports the validity of the applied MCDM models. The results identified high risk zones for policy focus and demonstrated the effectiveness of the multi-method approach in decision-making under uncertainty. Overall the rankings were found to be consistent, interpretable and statistically valid. It is strengthening their application in real-world traffic safety management.
Discussion
The FIR system provides an evaluation by integrating the outcomes of five MCDM methods such as TOPSIS, VIKOR, WASPAS, CODAS and COPRAS. This approach mitigates the inconsistencies among individual methods and yields a final ranking that captures the overall performance of each city. According to the FIR results Chennai stands out with the 1st rank and maintaining exceptional scores across all five methods. It is making that as the best performing city. Delhi follows closely in 2nd position which consistently placed in the top 10 by each method. Indore ranked 3rd which shows uniform excellence being ranked 1st by WASPAS and 2nd by TOPSIS and CODAS. Bengaluru secures the 4th FIR rank and indicating strong infrastructural service based efficiency. Dhanbad and Thrissur ranked 4th and 5th respectively. It is maintaining high positions across all models emphasising their consistent quality. Mumbai at 7th place performs steadily with all method based rankings placing it within the top 10.
On the other end of the spectrum Lucknow is the lowest-ranked city with an FIR of 53 consistently placed last by every method. Ghaziabad and Kanpur with FIRs of 52 and 50 also exhibit poor performance across all criteria suggesting systemic issues in their evaluated parameters. Coimbatore holds the 48th FIR rank matching low ranks across TOPSIS, VIKOR, WASPAS and CODAS. Madurai and Nagpur follow with FIRs of 47 and 46 respectively and confirming the underwhelming evaluations by all individual methods. Amritsar though ranked 1st in VIKOR has a final FIR of 7 as it ranked lower in other methods such as COPRAS (6) and WASPAS (5) which shows how FIR effectively balances extremes. Kannur, Kozhikode and Ranchi with FIRs of 15, 14 and 15 respectively demonstrate variability in rankings but end up in the upper middle segment due to the fuzzy inference process averaging their performance. Jaipur, Jabalpur and Patna fall in the mid FIR range of 21 to 32 reflecting average performance across the board.
Tiruchirappalli and Durg Bhilainagar receiving better individual rankings which placed \(43\textrm{rd}\) and \(42\textrm{nd}\) respectively in FIR due to inconsistent scores from certain methods. Jodhpur given a very low rank by COPRAS \((53\textrm{rd})\) achieves a \(32\textrm{nd}\) FIR due to stable rankings in the other methods showing how FIR neutralizes the effect of outliers. Vijayawada and Vishakhapatnam both holding a \(42\textrm{nd}\) and \(44\textrm{th}\) FIR reflect steady low-to-moderate ranks across all methods. In the middle ranks Rajkot \((30\textrm{th})\), Raipur \((29\textrm{th})\) and Surat \((35\textrm{th})\) show moderate consistency without strong performance spikes. Kolkata despite being a major metropolitan city ranks 49th in FIR due to its consistently low placement across methods indicating performance concerns. Meanwhile Thrissur \((5\textrm{th})\) and Nasik \((9\textrm{th})\) shows how smaller cities can perform when evaluated on core efficiency metrics.
Results of the FIR ranking system provides a balanced insight into the performance of 53 Indian cities. It helps identify top cities for potential investment such as Chennai, Delhi and Indore. It is highlighting the areas in need of focused development efforts such as Lucknow, Ghaziabad and Kanpur. FIR offers a fair aggregated view by reconciling the strengths and weaknesses shown in each method. It ensures that no single evaluation criterion unfairly biases the final outcome. This makes FIR an essential tool in multi criteria city assessments and strategic planning. Figures 3, 4, 5, 6 and 7 shows the variations in the rankings of MCDM methods.
Comparative analysis
Comparative analysis is essential in evaluating the strengths and limitations of newly proposed methodologies by positioning them against existing models. It helps highlight advancements in accuracy, robustness and the ability to handle uncertainty in complex decision-making environments. In this study a comparison is made with recent works that have utilised the advanced fuzzy MCDM methods and including IVT2FS. While these approaches have contributed to modeling expert uncertainty they often lack the ability to represent neutrality and fail to incorporate dynamic weighting mechanisms. The proposed method based on T2PFS combined with a novel entropy measure which overcomes these gaps by capturing positive, neutral and negative assessments. This comparison shows the performance and balanced the decision support provided by this model in real world multi criteria evaluation problems. This study presents a crucial MCDM framework based on T2PFS integrated with a novel entropy measure. It addressed uncertainty, hesitation and neutrality in expert evaluations. By incorporating three dimensional information such as positive, neutral and negative. The proposed approach provides a realistic and comprehensive representation of human judgment. The use of entropy based weighting enhances the model’s adaptability by reflecting the importance of each criterion. Comparative analysis with existing fuzzy MCDM methods demonstrates the capability of the proposed model in producing balanced outcomes. This approach is valuable in complex decision making environments such as healthcare, risk analysis and public policy planning. It is working well where uncertainty and subjective assessments are prominent.
Sensitivity analysis
Sensitivity analysis conducted to examine the variation in the rankings by changing the parameter q which influences the normalised values associated with road accidents across 53 Indian cities. The parameter q ranges from 2 to 500 and is used to observe the robustness of the decision-making outcomes under different sensitivity levels. Each city evaluated using normalised values for multiple q levels which allowing a comparative view of cities respond to changing conditions. It observed that an increase in q values gradually rise across all cities which indicating a consistent progression. This behavior confirms that the model produces proportional changes in sensitivity levels. Kanpur, Lucknow and Prayagraj consistently showed the higher sensitivity values in the entire range which suggesting exposure to road accident risks. Cities such as Chennai, Delhi and Amritsar exhibited lower values that showing less sensitivity to the parameter changes. Aurangabad, Faridabad and Jodhpur exhibited identical trends which suggesting similarities in their road safety profiles.
These overlapping trends are useful for regional policy formulation. Raipur, Ahmedabad and Madurai displayed sharper increases in values that indicating higher sensitivity and potential vulnerability. The analysis reveal sudden spikes in values which reinforces the reliability of the evaluation model. The data shows the variation which demonstrating the model is free from distortions. The consistency in value increments in q levels affirms that the decision framework same in different scenarios. Cities maintaining their relative positioning in most cases which supporting the ranking stability. Cities with higher initial values are high when q value increases thereby validating the robustness of the applied method. Clusters of cities with similar patterns can be used for zonal interventions and road safety policies. No substantial deviations were found during the sensitivity changing. This suggests that the weightings computations are well calibrated. Uniform behavior across cities indicate that no input criterion dominates the outcome unfairly. Finally, this analysis confirms the credibility of the decision making method and ensuring dependable policy insights under parameter fluctuations. Hence, the results of the model are interpretable to changes in sensitivity settings.
The results reveal that cities with high rankings remain unaffected by parameter shifts. Figure 9 confirms the reliability of the criteria and the effectiveness of the decision-making models. Therefore the sensitivity analysis validates the robustness of the findings.

Limitations
The proposed T2PF framework offers a structure for assessing road accident factors in uncertain environments. The model relies on expert input which introduces subjectivity. It affects the consistency in results. The effectiveness of the approach is constrained by the availability of regional accident data in India.
- 
                    The computational complexity of T2PF aggregation, entropy and multiple MCDM calculations may require substantial processing time for continuous live traffic streams
- 
                    Real-time implementation would require constant integration of dynamic data sources such as sensors, IoT devices, GPS, traffic cameras and live accident feeds which were beyond the scope of the present study
- 
                    Data standardisation challenges arise due to heterogeneous formats across multiple traffic monitoring systems
- 
                    The current framework primarily uses structured historical government datasets rather than continuous streaming environments.
The computational complexity of handling IVT2PFNs pose challenges in real time applications. The current static structure lacks integration with predictive analytics and limiting the responsiveness to real time conditions. Future work can address the limitations by incorporating real time data sources, predictive models and adaptive weighting strategies. It will improve the decision making process for real world problems.

The current study presents a framework for road accident assessment using T2PFNs. But several parts open for further findings. Future research can focus on improving the ability of the model by incorporating real time data and predictive analytics. Integrating machine learning with fuzzy MCDM methods can lead to accurate accident risk forecasting.
- 
                    Future studies can enhance the model by incorporating real time traffic data, weather conditions, GPS based road usage and IoT sensor inputs to enable road accident risk assessment.
- 
                    The integration of fuzzy MCDM methods with machine learning models can improve accident prediction and automate the risk classification based on live data.
- 
                    Extending the model with GIS tools and applying it to different Indian states can validate its strength in various traffic conditions.
- 
                    The development of user friendly software can implement this fuzzy decision framework to assist traffic authorities in making decisions on road safety.
Developing region specific applications and decision support tools can join the gap between theory and field implementation. A detailed sensitivity analysis of operators and parameter variations can improve the reliability of outcomes. Overall future advancements can strengthen the model for large scale deployment in India’s road safety environment.
Conclusion
This study analysed road accident severity across 53 major cities in India using a comprehensive MCDM framework based on 35 critical evaluation criteria capturing road safety, infrastructure, accident frequency and emergency response dimensions. To ensure robustness, five prominent MCDM methods such as TOPSIS, VIKOR, WASPAS, CODAS, and COPRAS were integrated with five distinct aggregation operators including arithmetic, geometric, Einstein, Aczel-Alsina and harmonic means. A major theoretical contribution of this work is the development and formal proof of a novel distance measure theorem under the T2PF environment enhancing decision precision, uncertainty modelling and comparative evaluation capability. The proposed framework generated city-wise rankings and integrated them into a FIR enabling balanced and comprehensive assessment across all methods. According to the FIR results, Chennai emerged as the best-performing city by securing the \(1^{st}\) rank with exceptional consistency across all five methods, indicating superior performance in road safety, infrastructure, and emergency response. Delhi and Indore followed in \(2^{nd}\) and \(3^{rd}\) positions respectively while Bengaluru, Dhanbad, Thrissur, Mumbai and Nasik also demonstrated strong and stable safety efficiency. These top-performing cities can serve as benchmark models for transportation planning and policy design.
Finally, this study provides mathematically rigorous T2PF decision-making framework. It delivers actionable policy guidance for city-specific accident prevention and transportation reform. By integrating multiple MCDM methods, advanced aggregation operators, entropy and the proposed novel distance measure the framework improves interpretability, reliability, and practical applicability for real-world road safety governance, enabling authorities to strategically identify benchmark cities, prioritise critical risk zones and implement targeted interventions for safer urban transportation systems.

MADURAI: Five members of a family were killed after the car they were travelling in collided with several vehicles and flipped over multiple times on the Thumbaipatti highway near Melur in Madurai early on Monday. Four others sustained injuries in the collision and are undergoing treatment at government hospitals.
The deceased were identified as K Sriram (32), his wife Ranchana (27), their one-and-a-half-year-old daughter Kiruthika, Sriram’s brother K Balaji (28) and their mother K Rajamery (50), all hailing from Chennai.
Sriram’s father, V Kanagaraj (55), who was also in the car, two bike riders, R Murugan (40) and C Murugan (55) of Sivaganga, and the driver of another car, J Prakash (40) from Madurai, sustained injuries.
Police said the incident occurred around 6.30am when Sriram and his family were on their way to attend a family function in Thoothukudi. Sriram, who was at the wheel, lost control of the car and hit a two-wheeler, driven by R Murugan, from behind.
To avoid further collision, he diverted the car to the right, but crossed over the median and hit another car — driven by Prakash — coming from the opposite direction.
Car driver may have dozed off at the wheel
The car rolled over multiple times before coming to a stop. While five occupants of the car died on the spot, the sixth occupant, Kanagaraj, survived with multiple injuries. He is currently undergoing treatment at Government Rajaji Hospital in Madurai.
Both the bike occupants and Prakash were admitted to the Government Hospital in Melur. Police suspect that Sriram may have dozed off at the wheel, leading to the accident. On receiving information, the Melur police along with fire and rescue services personnel extricated the bodies and sent them for postmortem examination. District Collector Nishanth Krishna inspected the spot.

Chennai: A Chennai motor accident claims tribunal has awarded ₹1.04 crore as compensation to the family of a woman dentist who was killed in a road accident in Neelathanallur, near Thanjavur in 2022.
As the dentist travelled in a goods carrier (Tata Ace), the tribunal granted the award after deducting 10% towards contributory negligence on part of the dentist. “The tribunal holds that the deceased has also contributed to some extent to her death in the unfortunate accident occurred and the extent of contribution is calculated as 10%,” A B Naseer Ali, judge of the tribunal said, and passed the award on a petition moved by the deceased Imayavalli’s husband U Radhakrishnan, minor son R I Hemdev Dharshan, her father M Selvam, and mother S G Jothi seeking ₹45 lakh as relief for the death caused to the deceased in the road accident.
Representing the petitioners, advocate A S Bilal submitted that on Aug 15, 2022, Radhakrishnan was driving a goods carrier at around 2.00pm in which Imayavalli and others were seated in the rear side. While they were proceeding near Asoor Kulam, Neelathanallur, another goods carrier driven by B Rajesh coming from the opposite direction, driven in a rash and negligent manner collided against their vehicle. Imayavalli died on the spot while others sustained injuries.
Opposing the plea, the insurer of Rajesh’s vehicle Magma HDI General Insurance Co Ltd contended that there was a delay of 182 days in filing the petition. It further argued that the deceased being a dentist should not have traveled in the rear portion of a goods vehicle, which is permitted only for carrying goods. “If she had averted traveling there, she would not have died and so, reasonable contributory negligence should be added to the accident,” the insurer said.
Recording the submissions, the tribunal directed payment of ₹2.32 lakh each to the parents of the deceased and ₹50 lakh each to her husband and son. The share of the son was directed to be deposited in a nationalised bank until he becomes a major.

MADURAI: Five members of a family, including a one-and-a-half-year-old girl, from Chennai were killed and four injured in a road accident on the Madurai–Tiruchy highway near Melur early on Tuesday.
Rajakumari (51), her sons, Balaji (31) and Sriram (27), Sriram's wife Ranjana, and their one-and-a-half-year-old daughter Praneeka Sri died on the spot. Police and Fire and Rescue Services personnel rescued Rajakumari’s husband Kanagaraj (55) from the wreckage.
He sustained grievous injuries and was rushed to the Government Rajaji Hospital.
The family was travelling to Kovilpatti in Thoothukudi after Balaji's wife, Aishwarya, gave birth to a baby in Kovilpatti. Balaji had travelled separately by bus and joined his family near Villupuram to travel together.
When the car driven by Sriram reached near the Thumbaipatti bridge, it grazed a motorcycle carrying two men. It then hit the median, crossed into the opposite carriageway, overturned and rolled several times. Worsening the accident, another car travelling from Madurai towards Tiruchy collided with the vehicle.
Prakash of Madurai, who was travelling in the other car, and the two motorcyclists, Murugan (55) and Murugan (40) of SV Mangalam near Singampunari, sustained injuries. They were admitted to the Melur Government Hospital for treatment.
After a prolonged rescue operation, the bodies of the five victims were retrieved from the mangled car and sent to the Melur Government Hospital for post-mortem examination.
Madurai Collector M Nishanth Krishna and Superintendent of Police BK Arvind Devanathan inspected the accident site and later visited the hospital to console the injured and their relatives.
Traffic on the four-lane highway was diverted through the service road for several hours following the accident.

 The deceased have been identified as S Shyam, 25, of Augustine Pettai near Sungam, and V Vasanth Kumar, 28, of Puliyakulam.
 According to police, Shyam and Vasanth Kumar were going to buy a cake to celebrate the latter’s birthday, which is on Saturday. As they were travelling on the Pankaja Mill Road, a goods autorickshaw moving ahead of them turned right without signalling. The motorcycle rammed the goods autorickshaw and then dashed against the road median.
 Both the riders fell on the road. Shyam suffered severe head injuries and died on the spot. Vasanth Kumar sustained critical injuries on his chest and head and was admitted to Coimbatore Medical College Hospital, where he died on Saturday.

The Madras High Court has upheld a Motor Accident Claims Tribunal award of ₹2.92 crore to the family of an ISRO scientist who died after his motorcycle collided with a parked TATA Ace vehicle on Chennai's Outer Ring Road. Rejecting the insurer's plea that the deceased was partly responsible for the accident, the court held that the dangerous parking of the goods vehicle was the sole cause of the fatal crash.
Background of the Case
The case arose from an accident on December 31, 2019, when R.S. Pugazhenthi, a scientist at the Vikram Sarabhai Space Centre, was riding his motorcycle on the Minjur–Vandalur Outer Ring Road. His motorcycle struck the rear of a TATA Ace vehicle that had been parked on the left side of the road near the entry to an elevated stretch without adequate warning. He suffered fatal injuries at the scene.
His wife, minor son and mother approached the Motor Accident Claims Tribunal, Thiruvallur, seeking compensation. The Tribunal found the driver of the TATA Ace negligent and awarded compensation of ₹2,92,69,944 with interest. Tata AIG General Insurance challenged that finding before the High Court.
Court's Observations
A Division Bench comprising Justice C.V. Karthikeyan and Justice K. Rajasekar examined the evidence of the eyewitness, the driver of the parked vehicle, the FIR, photographs and the Motor Vehicle Inspection Report.
The court noted that the TATA Ace had been parked on the lane generally used by two-wheelers at the entry to an elevated section of the Outer Ring Road, where visibility was limited because of the slope.
The bench observed,
"The parking of TATA Ace vehicle was the root cause for the accident." 
It further held that although the deceased may have been travelling at a high speed, that alone could not amount to negligence because the Outer Ring Road was specifically designed for fast-moving traffic.
Rejecting the insurer's argument of contributory negligence, the court said,
"Fixing up of contributory negligence on the deceased would not be proper," adding that the vehicle had been parked at a crucial point on the road, triggering the collision.
The judges also took note of the police investigation, which resulted in a charge sheet against the driver of the parked vehicle, observing that there was no material to rebut those proceedings.
Decision
Finding no error in the Tribunal's conclusion on negligence, the High Court confirmed that the accident occurred solely because of the negligent parking of the TATA Ace vehicle. Since the insurer had not challenged the quantum of compensation, the court also upheld the compensation awarded by the Tribunal.
Accordingly, the Civil Miscellaneous Appeal filed by Tata AIG General Insurance Company Ltd. was dismissed, and the Tribunal's award remained unchanged.
Case Details
Case Title: Tata AIG General Insurance Co. Ltd. v. P. Ammu & Others
Case Number: CMA No. 1163 of 2024
Judge: Justice C.V. Karthikeyan and Justice K. Rajasekar
Decision Date: 03 June 2026

The Greater Chennai City Traffic Police (GCTP) has said that fatalities due to road accidents declined by over 10% in 2025 compared to 2024, as of December 23.
While 534 fatalities were recorded up to December 15 last year, the number reduced to 479 during the corresponding period in 2025. In addition, grievous hurt cases saw a substantial 64% drop, falling from 2,093 cases last year to 721 this year.
Road accidents rise
However, the total number of road accidents increased to 3,981 this year from 3,753 last year, marking a rise of 6.07%. Police officials said efforts are under way to bring accident numbers down and maintain them at the previous year’s level.
Greater Chennai City Police Commissioner A. Arun said fatalities had been reduced by over 10% compared to last year, and grievous hurt cases had dropped significantly. He added that the GCTP would continue its efforts to reduce accidents and ensure road safety as a top priority.
According to statistics provided by the GCTP, during the corresponding period last year up to December 22, 2024, 3,753 accidents were recorded, resulting in 534 fatalities. Grievous injury cases stood at 2,140, simple injury cases at 941, and 138 accidents were reported with no injuries.
As of December 22, this year, a total of 3,981 accidents were reported, resulting in 479 fatalities. Of these, 754 cases involved grievous injuries, 2,630 involved simple injuries, and 118 were reported as no-injury accidents, where vehicles were damaged but occupants were unharmed.
This year, most motor accidents occurred during peak hours between 9 a.m. and 12 noon, with 711 incidents reported during this period. This was followed by 615 accidents between 3 p.m. and 6 p.m., and 602 accidents between 6 p.m. and 9 p.m.
Fewer accidents on weekends
Accidents were comparatively fewer on Saturdays and Sundays than on weekdays, owing to strict enforcement measures. Statistics show 588 accidents on Saturdays and 578 on Sundays.
Two-wheeler accidents accounted for a major share of road mishaps, with 1,573 such accidents reported and 2,076 persons either injured or killed. In addition, 878 cars, 378 autos, 176 buses, 280 lorries, and 275 vans were involved in road accidents.
Additional Commissioner of Police (Traffic) G. Karthikeyan said the GCTP has undertaken various steps and remedial measures to reduce road accidents and enhance road safety across the city through increased enforcement, patrolling, and awareness activities. He added that the GCTP creates impactful awareness among road users by urging the public to maintain road discipline, follow safety guidelines, use protective gear, and educate themselves on road safety.
In coordination with experts, the GCTP has facilitated several training programmes for police personnel on technological approaches to accident reduction, along with workshops and safety education programmes for schoolchildren, bus drivers, and delivery agents. In addition to awareness campaigns, the GCTP has strengthened its enforcement strategy by booking more cases for over speeding, drunken driving, and riding without helmets through manual checks and technological initiatives such as ANPR cameras, 2D speed radar systems, and vehicle interceptor systems across Chennai city.
Joint Commissioner of Police (South) P. Vijayakumar said, “We are constantly monitoring accidents through our real-time monitoring system. If the accident rate rises in any particular area, the concerned officer will be asked to explain the cause or any lacunae in enforcement. We are analysing whether accidents are due to human error or infrastructure issues. Furthermore, the GCTP is continuously taking steps to improve road conditions, signage, and lighting at identified hotspots and accident-prone zones. These collective efforts have led to a significant reduction in road accident fatalities compared to last year in Chennai city.”

Road accident fatalities have decreased by 12% in 2025 as on August 3 when compared to the same period in 2024 in city limits, according to statistics provided by Greater Chennai TrafficPolice (GCTP). This was made possible by a series of steps taken by the GCTP.
As many as 316 fatalities occurred last year till August 3. This has been brought down to 278 fatalities.
Additional Commissioner of Police, Traffic, G. Karthikeyan said, “We have undertaken various steps and remedial measures to reduce road accidents and enhance road safety across the city through increased enforcement, patrolling, and awareness activities. Also, GCTP creates impactful awareness among the road users by asking the public to maintain road discipline, follow safety guidelines, use protective gear and educate themselves on road safety.”
In coordination with experts, GCTP has facilitated training programmes for police personnel towards technological approaches for accident reductions and through workshops and safety education programs for schoolchildren, bus drivers, and delivery agents, he said.
Last year, 534 fatal road accidents were reported in the city. Of them, 380 involved two-wheelers amounting to 71%. Similarly, 66 fatal accidents involving four wheelers were reported.
Of the 278 fatal accidents that have been reported so far this year, 214 of them involved two wheelers and 29 of them involved four wheelers.
The GCTP has strengthened its enforcement strategy by booking more cases against over speeding, drunken driving,and riding without helmet through manual checks and technological initiatives like ANPR cameras, 2D - Speed Radar System and Vehicle interceptor system throughout the city. The GCTP booked 13,389 cases for drunk driving last year and 13,185 cases so far this year. K. P. Subramanian, an expert in urban engineering said, “It’s heartening to note that the rate of accidents in Chennai has reduced by 12% due to multi-pronged strategies adopted by the traffic police. As it is the institution in-charge of in charge of traffic rules enforcement, accident investigation, including accident data collection, data analysis, and drawing of inferences, the GCTP should validate their findings through an independent and impartial third-party audit,” he said.
B. Ramdasse, road safety expert, said the GCTP periodically implements traffic diversion in various high traffic volume roads to ease the traffic congestion and this in turn helps in reducing the accidents at the junctions. “In coordination with Chennai Metro Rail Limited, trial runs are being successfully implemented in junctions and other places where Metro works are happening to reduce accidents,” he said.
Published - August 15, 2025 12:58 am IST
summary: 12% reduction in road accident fatalities in Chennai city, say Traffic Police The Hindu
title: 12% reduction in road accident fatalities in Chennai city, say Traffic Police - The Hindu

But the situation turned worse as the mother fell on the left, and Niralya fell onto oncoming traffic and went under the wheel of the lorry, said police.

A senior police officer in the know of the investigation said the van, which had 12 passengers and the driver, is suspected to have veered off the 13th hairpin bend, when the driver attempted to negotiate the curve without reducing the speed.
The officer said the van’s driver Muhamed Fasith (21) was at the wheel when the accident took place. Mr. Fasith and Shahadin (11) are undergoing treatment at the Coimbatore Medical College Hospital (CMCH), according to the officer. Noushad Ali (39), who was admitted to the hospital with the duo, died without responding to treatment early on Wednesday (April 22, 2026). Another injured, Masneen (10), had been shifted to a hospital in her native district.
Meanwhile, the police officer refuted reports which said that Noushad, a school bus driver, drove the van at the time of the accident. “There is no evidence, yet, to state that Noushad drove the van. Our primary suspicion is that inexperience of the driver coupled with speeding at the hairpin bend led to the accident,” added the officer. The police shifted the van from the accident spot.
An official from the Regional Transport Office, Pollachi, said the van was completely damaged in the impact of the fall from the 13th hairpin bend to the ninth hairpin bend. “We could only carryout site inspections as the vehicle could not be examined due to heavy damage. We are also unable to ascertain whether the vehicle had any technical glitch like a brake failure,” said the official.
